title: Scan Repair Local
user: Readers and researchers with scanned books or archival PDFs who need usable text without uploading sensitive material.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker has philosophy texts available only as scans and says classic OCR is inferior to copying pages into ChatGPT; the thread has 57 comments.
A user asks for automatic sharpening and contrast because there is no handy workflow for blurry scanned PDFs.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests; scan quality is an immediate blocker to reading/searching, not a nice-to-have.
current_workaround: Manually crop pages, use a cloud LLM/OCR, or run several disconnected image and OCR tools.
incumbents_and_gap: OCRmyPDF, Tesseract, Adobe Acrobat, and Stirling PDF cover pieces of the workflow; none makes local scan diagnosis, repair, OCR, and per-page confidence review a small guided task.
smallest_useful_product: Offline desktop/PWA tool that detects skew/blur/contrast, previews reversible repairs, runs local OCR, and exports searchable PDF plus Markdown with page references. Non-goals: cloud document storage, LLM chat, or perfect handwriting recognition.
success_measure: In a 20-document pilot, 70% of users export a searchable document with fewer than five manually flagged pages.
monetization: one-time — private local conversion has clear value and should not require a recurring upload service.
constraints: Keep files on device by default; bundle or document OCR language packs; preserve originals; clearly label OCR uncertainty; do not imply archival-grade accuracy.
why_distinct: It is a local quality-and-confidence workflow around OCR, not another generic PDF toolbox or AI summarizer.

title: Redaction Proof
user: People sending converted or redacted PDFs who need evidence that hidden text, metadata, and removable overlays are not still present.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user calls wkhtmltopdf painful and asks for a current open-source HTML-to-PDF workflow; 51 comments show the conversion path remains unsettled.
A reported automated/OCR redaction leaves text readable by copy and paste in the output PDF.

recurrence: Conversion and redaction failures arise independently; a false sense of redaction is high-severity because it can disclose private information.
current_workaround: Trust a PDF editor's visual overlay, manually copy/paste-test pages, or flatten/reprint documents without a verification record.
incumbents_and_gap: Acrobat, qpdf, and Stirling PDF can transform files, but their normal workflow does not produce a simple pass/fail proof that text layers, annotations, attachments, actions, and metadata were removed.
smallest_useful_product: A local drop-zone that inspects a PDF, flags recoverable text/objects/metadata behind requested redactions, creates a sanitized copy, and emits a machine-readable verification report. Non-goals: legal advice, cloud signing, or document editing.
success_measure: At least 95% of seeded hidden-text and metadata cases are detected in a regression corpus, with no original file uploaded.
monetization: one-time — it is an occasional, risk-sensitive verification utility.
constraints: Must make no legal guarantee; retain nothing by default; safely parse hostile PDFs in a sandbox; preserve an audit hash rather than document contents.
why_distinct: The product verifies a security property of an output file rather than competing as a broad PDF editor.

title: Longform PDF Check
user: Technical writers and consultants exporting long Markdown reports who need a PDF whose table of contents, code blocks, links, page breaks, and metadata survive conversion.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user with a couple-hundred-page Markdown file says md2pdf, Pandoc, and LaTeX paths fail their requirements for code, TOC, and internal links; 35 comments.
A PDF metadata edit reports success but creation/modification dates do not apply, illustrating that output-file correctness is not visible from the conversion UI.

recurrence: Long technical exports fail on several independent output properties; the failure is usually discovered only after delivery.
current_workaround: Trial multiple Pandoc/LaTeX themes, visually inspect dozens of pages, and hand-fix PDF metadata or broken links.
incumbents_and_gap: Pandoc, Typora, Quarto, and browser print produce PDFs; none is focused on validating a long document against an explicit delivery checklist after conversion.
smallest_useful_product: CLI plus local HTML report that accepts Markdown and a generated PDF, checks heading/TOC targets, internal and external links, code-block overflow, empty pages, page-count drift, and selected metadata. Non-goals: a Markdown editor or proprietary typesetting engine.
success_measure: On a 50-fixture corpus, it catches 90% of seeded broken links, overflow, missing metadata, and TOC mismatches before distribution.
monetization: free — CI-friendly validation benefits from an open local core; paid templates/support could follow.
constraints: Do not fetch remote links by default; parse PDFs defensively; checks must distinguish warnings from hard failures; respect font licenses in sample templates.
why_distinct: It is a delivery preflight for generated documents, not a new Markdown-to-PDF converter.

title: Android Backup Receipt
user: Android owners moving phones or relying on self-hosted backup who need to know which local photos, files, and app-export folders are actually recoverable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN simply asks how people back up Android; it drew 82 comments, indicating no obvious trusted default workflow.
Nextcloud Android's Auto Upload issue has 122 comments and 90 reactions around a local file no longer being found.

recurrence: Broad backup uncertainty plus a heavily reacted upload-failure report; the loss is irreversible personal data.
current_workaround: Assume a cloud photo app succeeded, copy selected folders by USB, or discover missing files while restoring a new phone.
incumbents_and_gap: Google One, Nextcloud, Syncthing, and OEM migration tools perform transfers but do not issue a user-readable, destination-independent coverage receipt for selected folders and media types.
smallest_useful_product: Android app that inventories chosen SAF folders, computes a privacy-preserving manifest, compares it with an attached USB/WebDAV/S3 destination, and produces a dated restore receipt with missing/changed counts. Non-goals: backing up protected app data, bypassing Android permissions, or operating a cloud.
success_measure: In a device-migration pilot, 90% of chosen files are accounted for by a receipt and participants identify any missing category before wiping the old device.
monetization: one-time — a migration/assurance tool should work with a user's existing storage.
constraints: Use Android Storage Access Framework only; never claim full-device backup; hash efficiently under battery limits; encrypt destination credentials; disclose media metadata handling.
why_distinct: It verifies backup coverage across destinations rather than trying to replace every Android backup provider.

title: Media Fidelity Audit
user: Families and photographers self-hosting a photo library who need proof that originals—not flattened or altered derivatives—made it into the archive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user with a large family-photo collection asks for the 2025 self-hosted stack with local AI; the post has 33 comments.
An iOS user reports 240fps slow-motion video is flattened to 30fps during what they expected to be a backup; 23 comments.

recurrence: Self-hosted photo demand meets a concrete fidelity-loss report; an archive that silently changes media is not a backup.
current_workaround: Trust the photo-library UI, retain a second unverified copy, or compare filenames and sizes manually after an import.
incumbents_and_gap: Immich, PhotoPrism, Google Photos, and Syncthing manage libraries or transfers; none makes a cross-library original-versus-archive fidelity audit the primary simple workflow.
smallest_useful_product: Local CLI/desktop app that compares a camera export or mounted source to an archive, reports byte/hash matches plus codec, frame rate, EXIF, Live Photo pairing, and missing originals, then writes a portable manifest. Non-goals: photo hosting, face recognition, or transcoding.
success_measure: Detect 100% of intentionally altered codec/frame-rate/metadata fixtures and produce a clean manifest for 10,000 assets in under one hour on consumer hardware.
monetization: one-time — archive verification is periodic and works best without a hosted account.
constraints: Read-only by default; no photo upload; account for sidecars and platform-specific Live Photo pairs; document that hashes do not assess visual quality.
why_distinct: It protects original-media fidelity across tools instead of being another photo-library clone.

title: Reading Comfort Profiles
user: Knowledge workers with low vision who need readable text, code, tables, and density settings across web-based work apps without changing every site manually.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker progressively losing eyesight asks what tools can support Office 365, Teams, Google Docs, Confluence, Salesforce, and PowerBI.
A low-vision desktop user says uniform zoom does not solve typography balance among body text, headings, inline code, lists, and code blocks.

recurrence: Two independent low-vision reports identify the same gap: global zoom is too blunt for dense knowledge-work interfaces.
current_workaround: OS magnifier, browser zoom, reader mode where available, and repeated per-site CSS/font changes.
incumbents_and_gap: Browser zoom, Windows Magnifier, ZoomText, and reader modes help globally or on articles; they do not offer quick, per-domain profiles for semantic text density in application UIs.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension with keyboard-switchable per-domain profiles for base font, line height, code font, contrast, cursor/focus visibility, and optional table spacing; all settings stay locally. Non-goals: screen reader replacement, page scraping, or AI rewriting.
success_measure: In a four-week accessibility pilot, at least 70% of participants retain profiles on three or more work domains and report fewer manual zoom changes per day.
monetization: free — accessibility core should be broadly available; optional paid managed policy tooling is possible later.
constraints: Must not break keyboard navigation or application layouts; follow WCAG guidance; no browsing-history collection; provide a one-key disable switch.
why_distinct: It treats readability as a saved, semantic per-workflow preference rather than a single global magnification setting.

title: Zoom Workflow Check
user: Small web teams and accessibility consultants who need to show whether a real keyboard workflow remains operable at 200–400% browser zoom.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN developer says accessibility implementation is inaccessible without a dedicated a11y/UX team and asks which tools help; 8 comments.
A Kibana issue states that at 400% zoom a flyout prevents low-vision users from interacting with its content.

recurrence: Accessibility tooling is hard for small teams, while a concrete 400%-zoom failure blocks a workflow rather than merely reducing polish.
current_workaround: Run generic automated audits, resize a browser by hand, and discover clipped dialogs in user reports.
incumbents_and_gap: axe, Lighthouse, and Pa11y find many static issues but are not a compact, replayable test of tab order, focus visibility, clipping, and reachability through a named high-zoom workflow.
smallest_useful_product: Playwright-compatible CLI that records a short keyboard path, reruns it at 200% and 400%, captures focused-element visibility/clipping/scrollability, and outputs a visual HTML diff. Non-goals: legal conformance certification or a general test platform.
success_measure: On a seeded suite of high-zoom failures, it flags at least 90% of unreachable or obscured focused controls with fewer than 10% false positives.
monetization: free — a narrow open CLI invites CI adoption; paid consulting/report hosting can remain separate.
constraints: Use real browser zoom semantics; avoid claiming WCAG certification; screenshots may contain sensitive UI and must remain local/CI-scoped.
why_distinct: It tests a user journey under zoom, not just static markup rules or color contrast.

title: Bookmark Escape Hatch
user: People with years of browser and service bookmarks who need a reliable, inspectable export before changing tools or services.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN discusses the death of bookmark services such as Delicious and Pocket and asks how people return to saved links; 94 comments.
A user reports that exporting and then importing Linkwarden links fails, breaking the expected portability path.

recurrence: A high-comment community discussion and a concrete export/re-import failure show that users value saved links but cannot assume portability.
current_workaround: Keep browser exports, try imports blindly, use vendor-specific APIs, or abandon metadata and archived context during migration.
incumbents_and_gap: Browsers, Raindrop, Linkwarden, Pinboard, and Pocket exports exist, but users lack an independent tool that normalizes, checks, and proves what a migration will lose.
smallest_useful_product: Local browser/CLI utility that imports HTML/JSON/CSV exports, normalizes URLs/tags/dates, detects duplicates and malformed records, produces a vendor-neutral archive plus a destination-specific dry-run report. Non-goals: another hosted read-later service or content scraping.
success_measure: For supported exports, 99% of valid input records round-trip through the neutral format, and the report identifies every unsupported field before import.
monetization: free — portability needs trust and should be runnable locally; paid migration support is optional.
constraints: Process exports locally; avoid downloading protected article content; use documented formats; preserve source attribution and archive timestamps where present.
why_distinct: It is an escape and verification utility across bookmark products, not a destination bookmark manager.

title: Time Ledger Import Guard
user: Freelancers moving between self-hosted or client-required time trackers who need to import historical work logs without silently duplicating billable entries.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2025 professional time-tracking post explicitly targets freelancers and remote developers with timestamped, verifiable work records.
A Solidtime user reports that importing an exported ZIP into a fresh instance duplicates time entries on a second import.

recurrence: Professional tracking and import integrity appear independently; duplicate entries can create billing disputes or corrupt productivity history.
current_workaround: Hope an import is idempotent, de-duplicate in spreadsheets, or abandon historical data when switching trackers.
incumbents_and_gap: Toggl, Harvest, Kimai, Solidtime, and Clockify track time; their importers are product-specific and rarely show an auditable before/after reconciliation plan.
smallest_useful_product: Local CSV/JSON converter that maps time entries to a canonical ledger, builds deterministic fingerprints, previews duplicates/conflicts/time-zone shifts, and emits an import file plus a signed reconciliation report. Non-goals: time capture, invoicing, payroll, or hosted sync.
success_measure: On migration fixtures, it identifies 100% of duplicate/replayed entries and keeps valid adjacent entries with the same duration distinct.
monetization: one-time — users need it during migration or audit periods, not as a subscription tracker.
constraints: Keep client/project labels local; document time-zone normalization; never create invoices or make legal billing assertions; support only documented import formats.
why_distinct: It is a neutral reconciliation layer for time data, not another timer.

title: Calendar Snapshotter
user: People who plan in calendars but need a recoverable, diffable local history when schedules shift or a calendar provider is unavailable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A planner builder says conventional planners assume schedules stay fixed even though life changes; its product premise is automatic adaptation.
A calendar user requests configurable periodic exports to ICS, including retention count, frequency, and export time.

recurrence: Both sources point to calendars as changing operational data rather than a static schedule; users need recovery and visibility over changes.
current_workaround: Trust provider history, occasionally export an ICS manually, or duplicate events into a second calendar.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar, Outlook, CalDAV clients, and KashCal manage events; automatic local snapshots with human-readable calendar diffs and one-event restore are rarely a focused lightweight layer.
smallest_useful_product: Local scheduled CalDAV/ICS snapshot utility that stores encrypted versioned ICS files, summarizes added/moved/cancelled events, and restores selected events to an export file. Non-goals: calendar hosting, scheduling AI, or sending invitations.
success_measure: A pilot user can identify and restore a deliberately changed or deleted event from a snapshot in under two minutes.
monetization: one-time — calendar continuity should not depend on another subscription.
constraints: Encrypt stored credentials and event data; handle recurrence/time zones correctly; use CalDAV/ICS standards; avoid sending any event content to a third party.
why_distinct: It adds local version control and recovery to calendars rather than competing as another planner.

title: Local Data Finder
user: Professionals with years of notes, correspondence, code, and documents spread across folders and exports who need private cross-source retrieval with an inspectable source trail.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user has 20 years of notes, correspondence, code, and documentation across cloud services and says cross-service search is impractical.
A Joplin issue reports stale API search results after sync, underlining that even one personal knowledge source can give unreliable retrieval.

recurrence: Long-term personal data fragmentation is explicit, and stale indexing makes recall unreliable even inside a single app.
current_workaround: Search each cloud/service separately, manually export archives, or send an entire personal corpus to a hosted AI service.
incumbents_and_gap: Spotlight, Recoll, Everything, Devonthink, and personal knowledge apps search selected stores; a simple local ingest-and-evidence layer for ordinary exports across notes/mail/files remains fragmented.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop indexer for selected folders and explicit exports (Markdown, HTML, mbox, PDF text), with lexical search, filters, and every result linked to a local source path and extraction timestamp. Non-goals: cloud connectors, LLM chat, surveillance, or automatic deletion.
success_measure: In a 50-query personal-archive benchmark, users locate the source record for at least 80% of known facts without leaving the app.
monetization: one-time — privacy and local ownership are core to the proposition.
constraints: Index on-device; encrypt index option; make source scopes explicit; avoid interpreting mail attachments automatically; safely sandbox document parsers.
why_distinct: It prioritizes private source-grounded recall over an opaque AI layer or another note-taking system.

title: Import Reconciliation Ledger
user: Operations and finance admins loading CSV/template data into business systems who need to prove what transformed, matched, skipped, and changed before committing an import.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user asks how people clean and transform data before Salesforce, Workday, NetSuite, and other template-based imports; 18 comments.
A CSV import can silently merge a genuinely new transaction with an existing same-amount transaction even though preview shows it as new.

recurrence: Import preparation is an active cross-system concern, while a concrete silent-merge defect shows previews alone are not an adequate audit trail.
current_workaround: Clean sheets with formulas/scripts, trust an import preview, take screenshots, and manually compare totals afterward.
incumbents_and_gap: Excel/Sheets, OpenRefine, ETL platforms, and each SaaS import wizard transform data; lightweight local tools rarely create a persistent row-level reconciliation ledger that non-engineers can review.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web app that maps CSV columns, applies visible transforms, computes before/after totals and stable row fingerprints, records match/skip/create decisions, and exports both destination CSV and an immutable review report. Non-goals: direct SaaS writes, cloud ETL, or autonomous field guessing.
success_measure: In pilot imports, admins can account for 100% of source rows and identify every seeded silent merge or dropped row before upload.
monetization: one-time — local, auditable prep work suits project-based data migration and avoids exposing business data.
constraints: Never upload spreadsheets; use deterministic transforms; protect PII in saved projects; do not claim accounting correctness; support a limited documented CSV scope first.
why_distinct: The core artifact is a human-reviewable reconciliation ledger, not another generic spreadsheet cleaner or AI mapper.
